title: Macron, Worst French President Ever?
author: Grégory Rzepski
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/Emmanuel_Macron_President_of_France_at_the_World_Economic_Forum_Annual_Meeting_2026-680x435.jpg)

Photograph Source: World Economic Forum - [CC BY-SA
4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)

Emmanuel Macron leaves the Élysée in eight months. And, in keeping with the
political journalism tradition whereby last-minute criticism apparently makes
up for a decade of deference, the brickbats are coming thick and fast. _The
Economist_ , having once regarded him as the ‘saviour of Europe’, now mocks a
‘lame duck’ president. Two Parisian courtiers have devoted a book to ‘the
story of an exceptional man … who screwed things up in an exceptional way’.
Alain Minc, mouthpiece of the liberal elite and once the president’s advisor,
has called him ‘the Fifth Republic’s worst president’
([1](https://mondediplo.com/2026/09/01edito#nb1)).

As the Latin tag has it, _Ingratis servire nefas_ – ‘There’s nothing to be
gained from serving the ungrateful.’ And ungrateful they certainly are: since
2017 Macron has largely followed the recommendations of the Minc report (1994)
and the commission chaired by Jacques Attali (2008), on which he served as
deputy rapporteur. He has likewise followed the defence spending
recommendations of the European Union and NATO.

More than any of his predecessors, Macron has stripped French diplomacy of the
vestiges of independence that used to set it apart. Paris has adopted Kyiv’s
Russia policy, Washington’s Venezuela policy, Abu Dhabi’s Iran policy and
Berlin’s trade policy. It no longer has an Africa policy, since the Sahel
states sent its army packing.

Macron has also completed the transformation of the state into a Committee of
Private Safety, ensuring record dividends for shareholders
([2](https://mondediplo.com/2026/09/01edito#nb2)). Of the EU’s 27 member
states, France has become a haven for speculative funds that now control
thousands of businesses, including some of the country’s most prestigious
companies. The social security system no longer aspires to provide for each
according to their needs, while resource-starved public services are turning
into a nightmare for employees and users.

Macron has been the virtuoso exponent of the liberal, Atlanticist extreme
centre. But he’s been playing out of time. A champion of globalisation and
transcending traditional politics, he did not foresee either the former’s
demise or the latter’s return. His supply-side strategy, discredited by the
international resurgence of sovereignty and economic planning, has failed.
Unemployment is on the rise, growth is stagnant. The trade deficit remains
high, while almost half of France’s consumption-based carbon footprint
consists of emissions generated abroad. The public finance deficit is used to
justify France’s shortage of firefighters and firefighting aircraft.

As his country burned last month, Macron was photographed speeding across the
water on a jet ski – a fitting image for a presidency ending with a headlong
rush on two fronts. The first is Ukraine, which is intended to reunite his
camp after his disastrous dissolution of the National Assembly in 2024 and
give a boost to Europe’s defence industry in the name of strategic autonomy.
But it comes with the risk of triggering massive German rearmament (see
special report, in this issue) or even a confrontation with Russia.

The second is the erosion of civil liberties, which has been under way for
several years, and has been reinforced by the recent appointment of a
reactionary, François-Noël Buffet, as Defender of Rights, and government
support for a presumption that police officers act in legitimate self-defence.

Five years ago, Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner for the 2027 presidential
election said of Macron in _Le Figaro_ , ‘Here’s a man who has suppressed
freedoms … with unprecedented violence … And then he comes along and says
Marine Le Pen is a threat to individual freedoms and democracy. It’s a joke.’

In May 2017 president-elect Macron said of Le Pen’s voters, ‘I will do
everything to ensure that they no longer have any reason to vote for the
extremes.’ Two terms later, we can see how well that’s turned out.

_Translated by George Miller._

diplomatique](https://mondediplo.com/2026/09/01edito)._
